questiontext.text:
In a proof by induction you write the statement for particular values of \(n\): for the base case, and for \(n = k+1\), which is what the induction step has to prove. Practise both on this statement about positive integers \(n\):

\[P(n):\quad {@lhsn@} = {@rhsn@}.\]

  1. Write out the statement \(P({@m@})\).

    [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

    Type * for multiplication and ^ for powers.

    [[feedback:prt1]]

  2. Complete the statement \(P(k+1)\).

    \(P(k+1):\quad {@lhsk@} +\) [[input:ans2]] \(=\) [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans2]] [[validation:ans3]]
    [[feedback:prt2]] [[feedback:prt3]]

generalfeedback.text:
1. \(P({@m@})\) is \(P(n)\) with every \(n\) replaced by {@m@}. It is a statement, an equation with a left-hand side and a right-hand side, not a number. Its left-hand side has {@m@} terms, following the pattern of \(P(n)\):

    \[P({@m@}):\quad {@pmtex@}.\]

    Both sides equal {@rval@}, so \(P({@m@})\) is true.

  2. \(P(k+1)\) is \(P(n)\) with every \(n\) replaced by \(k+1\). The sum runs one term further than in \(P(k)\): the new last term is the general term \({@gen@}\) with \(n = k+1\), which is {@tkp1@}. The right-hand side is \({@rhsn@}\) with \(n = k+1\):

    \[P(k+1):\quad {@lhsk@} + {@tkp1@} = {@rkp1tex@}.\]

    This is not \(P(k)\) with 1 added: that would give {@dr1@} on the right-hand side.

questionnote.text: {@sname@}, m = {@m@}: P(m) total {@rval@}; new term {@tkp1@}; right side {@rkp1@}
